It’s five answers to five questions. Here we go…
h
1. My coworker refuses to speak to me
q

My coworker is refusing to speak to me, and I am not sure what to do. For context, I was hired in the same role as her, but one year her junior. It is very normal in our field to have many people with the same role and speciality. We have the same speciality, but she’s better at certain elements of it than I am, and vice versa. We went to lunch before I joined and got along great! I genuinely thought we would be great friends and colleagues, and I really liked her.
q

However, the first week I joined, she came to my office and said she was threatened by my technical expertise and wanted to tell me that, because she was struggling to not isolate me professionally due to her jealousy. I didn’t know how to handle it, and said I wanted us to be good colleagues and didn’t think we needed to compete.
q

Since then, it has gotten worse. She basically won’t speak to me in the hallway or socially, and excludes me from any social events she organizes. This would be annoying but fine, except now she will not answer any messages from me on workplace questions or technical issues I’m not sure about. We don’t work directly together often, but we both work for the same managers.
q

Recently, she messaged our work groupchat to say there was a change to a model (which I had worked on) and she had the updated version. I requested she share the updated version, which she did in the chat. I then asked if we could walk through the changes so I could understand the reasons, as she mentioned it was weeks of work between her and other people (all of whom are more senior to us). She said no, she was too busy, and refused to explain the technical reason for the changes — which is an issue, because I work with this and I don’t fully understand the reason for all the changes. I’m reaching out to the manager on the model to see if we can walk through it instead.
q

But I’ve never had a coworker fully refuse to talk to me before, and I’m not sure what to do, and I feel totally crazy, like I’m back in high school. Is this enough to discuss with a manager? Do I try to address it with her directly? I haven’t had any conflict with her and she’s never expressed an issue with me, so it’s left me really frustrated and annoyed, like dealing with a professional Regina George.
p

You absolutely need to talk to your boss about what’s going on! It would be one thing if your coworker were just being chilly on a social level — although that too can become a workplace issue after a certain point, if it’s done with obvious hostility. But it’s 100% untenable for her to refuse to talk to you about work issues or answer work questions. If your manager is even halfway decent — if they’re even 10% decent — they’ll want to know this is happening so they can intervene. By refusing to answer your work questions, your coworker is flagrantly refusing to do part of her job and creating obstructions for your team. It’s not even remotely okay.
p

So yes, talk to your boss and tell her what’s going on. Be specific that your coworker started by ignoring you socially, which you didn’t love but felt you could work around, but that it’s progressed to now refusing to answer your work questions, and it’s causing XYZ work problems, and you’re not sure what to do.
h
2. My manager was irate that I talked to HR instead of her about an internal promotion
q
I still think about from time to time about an incident from more than a decade ago, and wonder if my boss was out of line or if I really mishandled the situation.
q

I was in my late twenties and working as a coordinator. I had been there for a year or so and was getting good feedback on my work. They decided to create a position in between me and the manager called senior coordinator, who would handle more exciting projects and supervise the two more junior coordinators.
q

I was a little nervous because I thought it was a natural next step, but my boss had not discussed the role with me. So I decided to reach out to our HR coordinator to find out if it was okay if I applied (I had never applied for an internal promotion at the time), and HR encouraged me to throw my hat in the ring.
q

The next day, my boss pulled me aside, breathing fire, and said that I had undermined her by asking HR about the role instead of her directly. She went on to say that this professional immaturity/lack of judgment was exactly why I was not ready for a senior position and she would have told me herself if she thought I was a candidate. I found having my motives questioned very upsetting — I believe I cried and am still annoyed I did that when being accused of immaturity — and protested that I thought I was supposed to go through HR with this sort of question and I wasn’t trying to undermine her in any way. Eventually she forgave me and I left, shaken.
q

This is long in the past but with the benefit of hindsight, I think I committed a minor faux pas but she wildly overreacted by accusing me of going to HR to deliberately undermine her authority. Can you give me your read on what happened here?
p

Her reaction was absurd. It would have been politically smarter for you to talk to your boss first (she was the one hiring for the position and she had the best read on your suitability for the role) but it wasn’t inappropriate for you to talk to HR, and it definitely wasn’t undermining to your boss in any way (and that was a bizarre angle for her to take on it). She should have used it as a mentoring moment to explain, “This is the kind of thing you can come to me about, and I’ll have a better read on the situation than HR because the position is on our team.” And she also should have understood that someone junior might not have known that or had any idea how internal applications work, and that asking HR for guidance is completely reasonable and not in any way inflammatory.
h
3. Can I ask for a different contact at the nonprofit I work with?
q

I’m an artist who sometimes contributes to silent auctions through a nonprofit, and I was wondering if you could advise how I can ask the organization, “Can I go through someone else and not Susie?” I’m not fluent in social media so I’ve asked Susie, their admin, to please ping me if there’s an upcoming auction I could contribute to; she said she will, and then often doesn’t or not in time. I find out about the auction much later. (I do try to keep up with when various orgs have their events, but I often miss them: social media is hard and this is supposed to be my hobby.)
q
I don’t think this is a deliberate ghost; my stuff does sell.
q
Is there any way I can ask to go through someone else, without being rude? Or how to handle it?
p

You can try, but if Susie is the main contact with artists for the auctions, someone else may be even less likely to remember than she is. It may just be that this organization’s systems aren’t set up to proactively contact artists; if they get enough interest just through social media, and especially if they’re small and under-resourced, this may just be the system that works best for them.
p

But you could try saying this to Susie: “I know we’ve talked about you pinging me if there’s an upcoming auction I could contribute to, but I haven’t been getting notifications, or they come too late for me to respond to. I know you’re swamped. Is there someone else there I could try to coordinate with?” Or, if you’re in contact with other staff members there, you could say a version of that to them. (“I know Susie is swamped, but it means I don’t hear about auctions in time to contribute. Is there another person who might be able to alert me when they’re happening?”) You could also suggest they consider an email list for artists who want to participate, so everyone could be alerted that way all at once; you’re almost certainly not the only person who misses announcements on social media.
p

That said, if their system is to push the info out via social media and expect people to find it there and it works fine for them (meaning that it gets them good enough outcomes, even if it’s not ideal), the most practical solution might just be to bookmark one of their social media profiles and check that page periodically yourself. You wouldn’t need to be fluent in social media to do that.
h
4. I’m stuck at part-time but doing more
q

I’ve been at my current job for nine years. I was initially hired as a part-time technician. Over the last nine years, I’ve worked to show that I can do more. At various times, some of my supervisors have requested more funds so that they can make me full time and put me on other projects, but the answer has always been “no” — I assume because it would be too expensive to budget for my benefits. Nevertheless, I’ve tried to grow within my position, in part because I love my work and in part because I’ve been hoping to demonstrate that my work is valuable and I should be full-time.
q

So over time I started mentoring students and handling more of the administrative tasks associated with running the program. When I started designing classes, it became obvious that my work did not fit within the scope of an hourly employee, so as a compromise, my role was transitioned to “part-time exempt” along with a pay raise, but they still kept me at 0.5 FTE.
q

Nine years ago when I took the job, I was fine with the job being part-time — the work wasn’t really anything I had to “take home” with me, so I had other part-time jobs to fill in the gaps. But over time I’ve had to turn down other work because I am too busy at my primary (but not full-time) job. I think I’m already working at least the equivalent of a 0.75 position, but I am not classified that way.
q

The thing is, I think if I push too hard on this, I think HR would agree with me and I’m afraid they’ll say “yes, you’re doing too much for part-time”… and take away all the best, most intellectually-stimulating, and most “resume-building” parts of my job. Which would make me miserable … and in this economy I can’t even guarantee that I’d be able to find other part-time work to make that loss worth it.
q

I know I probably should have been looking elsewhere this whole time, but I really didn’t want to work anywhere else and I liked that the folks at my current job knew what I was capable of and were willing to let me take on more responsibilities. Of course now, with the job market being what it is, I’m not sure I could even get another offer to use as leverage.
q
What do you think I should do? Tell them I need fewer responsibilities to bring my work back in alignment with 0.5 FTE? Get more serious about actively looking elsewhere? Something else?
p

I think you’ve got to assume that they’re not going to make you full-time or even three-quarters time, and take those off the table as options in your thinking. From there, what’s the outcome you’d most prefer — continuing as things are (including turning down some other part-time work because of the hours you’re working for this one) or working fewer hours but doing less of the work you enjoy?
p

To be clear, this isn’t about what’s fair, since what’s fair would be being compensated for all the work you’re doing; it’s about what’s practical and which outcome you’d be happiest with (or least unhappy with), while being realistic about what options are and aren’t available right now. And whichever of those you choose, you can also get more serious about actively looking elsewhere.
p

That said, can you talk to your boss about whether there’s a way to keep more of the work you like while getting your hours back to half-time? There might not be if the core work they need you to do is the stuff you don’t enjoy as much (and if the only reason you’re getting to do the other work is because it’s sort of a bonus to them but not their main need), but it’s worth raising the question.
h
5. I take more sick days than coworkers
q

I have several diagnosed health conditions that effectively make it so that work is more difficult and exhausting than for the average person. I manage to maintain a full-time job, but it’s hard, and I find myself needing more sick days than the average person. We’re not talking anything crazy, just more than other people in my company take — about one day a month. I’m okay taking them unpaid, but I’m worried that my job is going to see me as unreliable and that it could eventually cause me to get fired, passed over for promotions, etc. I’ve only been in this job for about six months and management hasn’t addressed my amount of time off yet, but I have a feeling that they’re going to.
q

What can I do to make sure my job is protected and that my sick days aren’t held against me? Can “please don’t fire me for calling out once a month” be an ADA accomodation? Do I need to use intermittent FMLA (once I’m eligible)? Something else?
q

For more context, I work in a blue collar, skilled manual labor type of job. There are a lot of people in my exact same role, so while it’s slightly inconvenient if I call out, it’s not a huge deal; it’s not like work can’t get done while I’m out. My company offers three weeks of combined PTO per year, and allows additional unpaid time off. There’s no official limit on unpaid time.
p
This is exactly what intermittent FMLA is for. It protects your job for exactly this sort of thing, and you should file for it!
